text.p: HSBC Holdings Plc, one of the world's biggest banking and financial services groups, Monday announced profits and dividends that were ahead of market expectations.
Pre-tax profit rose 13 percent to 2.623 billion pounds ($4.3 billion), while the first-half dividend was up 33 percent to 20 pence per share.
Analysts had forecast profits of between 2.32 billion and 2.48 billion pounds ($3.78 billion to $4.05 billion).
HSBC owns HongKong Bank in the Far East, Midland Bank in the UK, and its HSBC America's unit includes Marine Midland. It also has a controlling stake in Hang Seng Bank.

HSBC Chairman Sir William Purves said the group increased attributable, or net, profits to 1.757 billion pounds ($2.87 billion), 11 percent ahead of the comparable figure in 1996 "despite the adverse exchange rate translation impact of stronger sterling." The effect of exchange rates cut profits by around 70 million pounds ($114 million).
Purves said HSBC would consolidate recent its acquisitions in Latin America before looking at other markets, but noted that banking assets in mature markets look expensive.

"We don't have a shopping list. We look at opportunities all around the world as we've done and followed through in Latin America," Purves said in an interview. "We're not active in this field. We've done quite a lot this year and we'll see that consolidate before we get excited about other things."

Noting that all units had done well, Purves said HongKong Bank's results had been affected by a significant underwriting loss at its investment banking subsidiary, but he declined to give any details.
HSBC reported growth in loans, especially in Hong Kong, where the property market was buoyant, and in the UK, where corporate and mortgage lending was up.
Purves said the Hong Kong market was very competitive, with margins narrowing in the mortgage market. But he added that the bank had maintained its market share.
He said margins were under pressure at Midland Bank as well, though the bank had managed a sharp fall in cost income ratio.
Purves said currency turmoil in the Far East in recent months had not generated significant profits or losses but had added to volumes and volatility.
He said it was "business as usual" in Hong Kong since the territory was taken over by China, adding that the bank has complete confidence in Hong Kong's development.

He also said HSBC was also pleased with progress in mainland China, although he conceded tht this was slow and that foreign banks are probably not the Chinese government's main priority in terms of development.
